extracted.intended_audience: general readers and students of German cultural history, art history, and literature
extracted.subtask_short: history of German arts and letters
extracted.subtask_description: Expository historical account surveying standards, tastes, and judgments about German architecture, sculpture, painting, music, theatre, fashion, and literature from the relevant periods. The page discusses what was valued or criticized in each art form and reasons for artistic change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Architecture should preserve Gothic sublimity
rubrics_metrics.description: Architecture degenerates when the meaning of the Gothic style is no longer understood and when a tasteless imitation of the Roman style is brought into vogue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid slavish imitation of Roman/St. Peter's/Versailles models; retain the original spirit and sublimity of Gothic architecture rather than reducing it to superficial classical ornament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sculpture must be meaningful, not theatrical or trivial
rubrics_metrics.description: Sculpture that consists of theatrical attitudes, fat genii, coquettish nymphs, miniature turnery-ware, and microscopical curiosities is unmeaning and forced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer sculpture with expressive meaning and moral or aesthetic substance over decorative, frivolous, or excessively intricate curiosities (e.g., carved cherry-stones, golden carriages drawn by fleas) which signal decadence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collecting curiosities can foster scholarship
rubrics_metrics.description: The predilection for ancient gems promoted the study of the remains of antiquity, and collections of natural curiosities greatly facilitated the study of natural history.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While some collections are frivolous, judicious collecting of antiquities and natural specimens supports learned research and connoisseurship (examples: Stosch, Lippert, Winckelmann).

rubrics_metrics.name: Painting should balance study of nature with idealization
rubrics_metrics.description: Although painting became essentially German and nature was generally studied in the search after the beautiful, purely slavish imitation of nature limited higher artistic effects; a capacity to idealize remained important.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value careful study of nature and truthful detail (e.g., Denner, Gerhard Douw) while also seeking higher idealizing treatment for grand or historical subjects (as attempted by Claude Lorraine and others).

rubrics_metrics.name: Portraiture: grace vs idealization
rubrics_metrics.description: A good portrait combines grace and beauty but should be capable of idealizing the subject where appropriate; mere elegance without idealizing power is a limitation (Van Dyck graceful but 'incapable of idealizing').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portrait painters should aim not only for likeness and grace but also for the capacity to elevate and idealize when the subject calls for it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre and domestic painting must render truthful detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Domestic scenes and depictions of lower classes succeed through surpassing truth and attention to minute reality (e.g., Teniers, Ostade, Jan Steen).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For social and domestic groups, fidelity, truth to types, and careful detail are virtues; such works can capture social reality and attain high merit even when treating humble subjects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Animal and battle painting: technical fidelity to subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: Painters of horses, groups of horsemen, cattle-pieces, and sea-pieces excel by faithful delineation of their subjects (e.g., Wouvermann for horses; Berchem and Paul de Potter for cattle; Bakhuysen for seas and storms).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mastery of anatomy, movement, atmosphere, and the character of subject-matter is the measure of quality in animal and marine painting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Landscape painting as a higher style
rubrics_metrics.description: Landscape-painting alone gave evidence of a higher style: nature, when undesecrated by vulgarity, is sublimely simple and can be idealized or faithfully represented in a higher manner (Claude Lorraine vs northern natural garb).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Landscape artists may either idealize nature (as Claude) to achieve grandeur or represent the native, simple character of the scene (Everdingen, Ruysdael) to evoke national feeling; both approaches can be elevated if genuine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid degenerating landscape into mere ornament
rubrics_metrics.description: Landscape and other painting degenerated when reduced to mere ornamental 'flower-painting' or excessively minute, decorative pictures favored by merchant taste.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resist converting grand genres into mere decorative commodity; maintain expressive and compositional depth beyond surface prettiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Musical quality measured by depth, contrapuntal mastery, and expressive pathos
rubrics_metrics.description: Great music attains heights by technical mastery (Bach's 'colossal fugues'), melodic richness (Handel), depth and pathos in opera (Gluck), variety and melody in oratorio (Haydn), and perfection of operatic style (Mozart).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value compositional complexity, contrapuntal skill, expressive depth, melodic invention, and the successful fusion of these qualities in vocal and instrumental forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: National music should revive native talent rather than merely imitate foreign schools
rubrics_metrics.description: German musicians sought to extirpate the foreign and degenerate modes fostered by vanity and to give free scope to original native talent (rise through organists and inventions like the pianoforte).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage development of indigenous musical forms and talents rather than slavish imitation of Italian or French fashions; technical innovation and church music were important sources of national renewal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theatre must follow nature, not stilted French models
rubrics_metrics.description: German theatre improved when it abandoned the stilted Alexandrine and pseudo-Gallic imitation and took nature as a guide (Lessing, Iffland, Eckhof, Schroeder).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dramatic writing and staging should model natural behavior and truth rather than adherence to artificial verse forms and imported courtly fashions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literary taste: avoid Gallomania and bombast; prefer nature and classical learning
rubrics_metrics.description: Gallomania (slavish imitation of French models), bombast, and pedantic mixtures of languages degraded poetry; critics like Bodmer and Breitinger recommended nature, classics, and English example instead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Promote simplicity, naturalness, and study of ancient classics and English literature rather than faddish imitation of French court-poetry or needless linguistic ostentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic style should value harmony, simplicity, and national character
rubrics_metrics.description: Martin Opitz preserved the harmony of the German ballad; many poets sought to revive force and simplicity (e.g., Paul Gerhard) and to rescue popular old poetry (Herder).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poetry should aim for harmonious versification, simplicity of sentiment where appropriate, and engagement with national poetic traditions rather than artificial pomposity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry and drama should elevate public feeling and moral dignity
rubrics_metrics.description: Schiller spoke to the heart and became the champion of liberty, justice, and country; poets should restore self-respect and address public woes rather than indulging mere pleasure or aristocratic self-complacency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Valorize works that engage moral and political concerns and that stir collective feeling and dignity; avoid trivializing or justifying vice in the name of art (critique of Goethe's justificatory tendencies).

rubrics_metrics.name: Literary criticism should be independent, fearless, and rooted in native language
rubrics_metrics.description: Lessing's criticism drove French taste from the arena; he wrote in the native tongue, scorned patronage, and defended truth and independence (e.g., refusal to submit to censorship).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics should practice fearless, independent judgment, resist patronage and flattery, and promote native language and honest standards rather than pandering to foreign fashions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fashion should avoid deformity, unhealthiness, and inconvenience
rubrics_metrics.description: Fashion that produces monstrous forms (enormous perukes, padded headdresses, hoops, high heels, diminutive waists) is deforming and unhealthy; contemporaries vainly pointed this out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dress ought to be healthful, natural, and not a masquerade that parodies human form; critique or reform absurd and injurious modes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literary innovation must not sacrifice decency or naturalness
rubrics_metrics.description: Attempts to 'return to nature' that willfully overthrew limits of decency and custom (as by Heinse) disgraced genius; wild extremes and mere affectation are condemned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pursue innovation that respects human dignity and taste; avoid wanton transgression of decency under the pretext of artistic freedom.
